heading: Cold open
narration: High-carbon steel is plain carbon steel holding roughly 0.6 percent carbon or more by weight, and the only certain way to confirm it is a laboratory chemical analysis.

heading: Cold open
narration: That threshold is a convention found in reference handbooks published by ASM International, and the exact boundary shifts a little from one reference to another.

heading: Cold open
narration: Less than one part in a hundred of the metal decides whether a blade holds an edge or bends, and that small part is invisible to the eye, silent to a magnet, and only partly readable in a workshop.

heading: Title card
narration: How to tell if steel is high carbon?

heading: A magnet reads iron, never carbon
narration: Start with the test most people try first. Plain carbon steel is overwhelmingly iron, and iron at room temperature is strongly magnetic.

heading: A magnet reads iron, never carbon
narration: Adding a fraction of a percent of carbon does not switch that off.

heading: A magnet reads iron, never carbon
narration: So a magnet will cling to mild steel and high-carbon steel with no difference you could feel.

heading: A magnet reads iron, never carbon
narration: A magnet can't tell them apart. What a magnet can sometimes do is separate certain stainless steels, whose crystal structure makes them weakly magnetic or not magnetic at all, from ordinary carbon steels.

heading: A magnet reads iron, never carbon
narration: That is a useful sort, but it answers a different question. Colour, weight and the ring of a struck bar fail in the same way.

heading: A magnet reads iron, never carbon
narration: Two bars of mild steel and high-carbon steel have nearly identical density and look the same when freshly cut.

heading: A magnet reads iron, never carbon
narration: The difference you are hunting for is not in how much iron is present.

heading: A magnet reads iron, never carbon
narration: It is in how a small amount of carbon arranges itself inside that iron.

heading: A magnet reads iron, never carbon
narration: It helps to be precise about the category. Reference sources such as ASM International sort plain carbon steels by carbon content.

args.meaning: sort plain carbon steels by carbon content
args.boundary: Alloy steels deliberately add other elements

heading: A magnet reads iron, never carbon
narration: Low-carbon steel, often called mild steel, sits below roughly 0.3 percent carbon.

heading: A magnet reads iron, never carbon
narration: Medium-carbon steel runs from there up to roughly 0.6 percent carbon. High-carbon steel begins around that point and continues upward.

args.meaning: sort plain carbon steels by carbon content
args.boundary: Alloy steels deliberately add other elements

heading: A magnet reads iron, never carbon
narration: Go far enough, past roughly 2 percent carbon, and the material is usually called cast iron rather than steel.

heading: A magnet reads iron, never carbon
narration: Every one of those boundaries is a convention agreed for convenience, not a line drawn by nature, and different handbooks place them slightly differently.

args.meaning: sort plain carbon steels by carbon content
args.boundary: Alloy steels deliberately add other elements

heading: A magnet reads iron, never carbon
narration: The word "plain" matters too. Alloy steels deliberately add other elements, and those additions change how the metal sparks, hardens and looks, which complicates every workshop test that follows.

heading: A fraction of a percent rearranges the crystals
narration: To understand why the tests work at all, you need to know what carbon does.

args.caption: slowly cooled steel is almost entirely pearlite

heading: A fraction of a percent rearranges the crystals
narration: Carbon atoms are small enough to tuck into the gaps between iron atoms.

heading: A fraction of a percent rearranges the crystals
narration: When steel cools slowly from red heat, most of that carbon cannot stay dissolved, so it gathers into a hard iron carbide that forms fine layers alongside soft iron.

args.caption: slowly cooled steel is almost entirely pearlite

heading: A fraction of a percent rearranges the crystals
narration: Under a microscope, after polishing and etching, those layers appear as a fingerprint-like structure called pearlite.

heading: A fraction of a percent rearranges the crystals
narration: The more carbon, the more pearlite. At roughly 0.8 percent carbon, slowly cooled steel is almost entirely pearlite.

args.caption: slowly cooled steel is almost entirely pearlite

heading: A fraction of a percent rearranges the crystals
narration: This is one way metallurgists estimate carbon by eye: they cut a sample, polish it, etch it and judge how much of the surface is pearlite.

heading: A fraction of a percent rearranges the crystals
narration: It works only if the steel was cooled slowly, and it gives an estimate, not a measurement.

args.caption: slowly cooled steel is almost entirely pearlite

heading: A fraction of a percent rearranges the crystals
narration: Cool the steel quickly instead, by plunging it into water or oil, and the carbon has no time to escape.

heading: A fraction of a percent rearranges the crystals
narration: It stays trapped in the iron, forcing the crystal lattice into a strained, distorted form called martensite.

heading: A fraction of a percent rearranges the crystals
narration: That strain is what makes quenched steel hard. Up to a point, more trapped carbon means more strain and more hardness.

args.title: carbon controlling hardenability
stages: the carbon has no time to escape
args.conclusion: more trapped carbon means more strain and more hardness

heading: A fraction of a percent rearranges the crystals
narration: Low-carbon steel has too little carbon to harden much this way. High-carbon steel hardens dramatically.

heading: A fraction of a percent rearranges the crystals
narration: That single relationship, carbon controlling hardenability, is the hinge for almost every practical test you can do without a laboratory.

args.title: carbon controlling hardenability
stages: the carbon has no time to escape
args.conclusion: more trapped carbon means more strain and more hardness

heading: Producer POV
narration: Naming a public source doesn't guarantee a number is right. It makes the number inspectable — and therefore correctable.

heading: Sparks carry the signature of burning carbon
narration: The oldest workshop method is the spark test. You touch the steel to a grinding wheel and watch the stream of hot particles that flies off.

heading: Sparks carry the signature of burning carbon
narration: Each particle is a tiny fragment of metal heated as it tears away.

heading: Sparks carry the signature of burning carbon
narration: As it travels through air, the carbon inside reacts with oxygen and forms gas.

args.title: The spark test
steps: touch the steel to a grinding wheel
watch the stream of hot particles

heading: Sparks carry the signature of burning carbon
narration: When enough gas builds inside a glowing particle, it bursts, splitting the spark into forks and stars.

heading: Sparks carry the signature of burning carbon
narration: Mild steel throws long, fairly plain streaks with few bursts. As carbon rises, the bursts multiply, branching into bushy, crackling clusters.

args.title: The spark test
steps: touch the steel to a grinding wheel
watch the stream of hot particles

heading: Sparks carry the signature of burning carbon
narration: An experienced eye reads that density of bursts as a rough carbon gauge.

heading: Sparks carry the signature of burning carbon
narration: Notice what the method actually needs. It needs reference bars of known composition, ground on the same wheel, under the same light, by the same person, because the judgement is a comparison.

heading: Sparks carry the signature of burning carbon
narration: It can reliably separate low-carbon steel from high-carbon steel in plain steels.

heading: Sparks carry the signature of burning carbon
narration: It cannot give an exact percentage, and two steels a little apart in carbon can look much the same.

heading: Sparks carry the signature of burning carbon
narration: Alloyed steels remain an open problem: some alloying elements suppress the bursts or change the colour of the stream, so an alloy steel can masquerade as a lower or higher carbon grade.

heading: Sparks carry the signature of burning carbon
narration: The spark test is fast and cheap. It is a ranking, not a reading.

heading: Hardness only speaks after heat treatment
narration: The second workshop method uses that hardening behaviour directly. You heat a small piece until it glows and no longer attracts a magnet.

heading: Hardness only speaks after heat treatment
narration: Here the magnet finally earns its place, not as a carbon detector but as a thermometer: steel loses its magnetism close to the temperature where it is ready to harden.

heading: Hardness only speaks after heat treatment
narration: You then quench the piece and draw a file across it. On high-carbon steel the file skates, sliding across without biting, because the surface is now harder than the file can cut. On mild steel the file bites much as it did before.

heading: Hardness only speaks after heat treatment
narration: Read the result carefully. A skating file tells you the steel had enough carbon to harden.

heading: Hardness only speaks after heat treatment
narration: It does not tell you how much. Medium-carbon steel also hardens noticeably, and many alloy steels harden more deeply than plain high-carbon steel at all.

heading: Hardness only speaks after heat treatment
narration: The test also changes the sample, so it is unsuitable for anything you need to keep.

heading: Hardness only speaks after heat treatment
narration: Laboratories measure hardness with indentation instruments that press a shaped tip into the surface and record the mark, which turns "the file skated" into a value.

heading: Hardness only speaks after heat treatment
narration: Even then, hardness depends on carbon, heat treatment and alloying together, so it can only point toward carbon, never isolate it.

heading: Only chemistry returns a number
narration: To get an actual carbon content, a laboratory measures the carbon itself.

steps: burned in a stream of pure oxygen
The carbon leaves as carbon dioxide

heading: Only chemistry returns a number
narration: The standard approach is combustion analysis. A small sample is cut, often as chips or a pin, and burned in a stream of pure oxygen inside a furnace.

heading: Only chemistry returns a number
narration: The carbon leaves as carbon dioxide. An infrared detector measures how much carbon dioxide passes through, and from that the instrument calculates the carbon in the original sample.

args.title: combustion analysis
steps: burned in a stream of pure oxygen
The carbon leaves as carbon dioxide

heading: Only chemistry returns a number
narration: The step that makes this trustworthy is calibration. The instrument is checked against certified reference steels whose carbon content has been established with great care.

heading: Only chemistry returns a number
narration: NIST, the United States measurement institute, issues such certified reference materials, and ASTM International publishes standard test methods describing how these analyses should be carried out.

args.title: combustion analysis
steps: burned in a stream of pure oxygen
The carbon leaves as carbon dioxide

heading: Only chemistry returns a number
narration: A second laboratory technique is spark emission spectrometry. The sample's surface is struck with an electrical spark under a protective gas, and the light given off is split into its wavelengths.

heading: Only chemistry returns a number
narration: Each element emits at characteristic wavelengths, so the strength of the carbon lines indicates the carbon content.

heading: Only chemistry returns a number
narration: Again, the reading is only as good as the reference steels used to calibrate it.

heading: Only chemistry returns a number
narration: Notice the chain of trust. NIST certifies the reference, ASTM International describes the method, ASM International publishes the classification ranges you compare the result against. Each link is a public body whose work you can inspect.

heading: Only chemistry returns a number
narration: There is a trap here worth knowing. Handheld X-ray fluorescence analysers are common in scrap yards and inspection work, and they identify many alloying elements quickly.

heading: Only chemistry returns a number
narration: But carbon is a very light element, and its signal is too weak for these instruments to measure reliably.

heading: Only chemistry returns a number
narration: A mild steel and a high-carbon steel that differ mainly in carbon can produce almost identical X-ray fluorescence readings.

heading: Only chemistry returns a number
narration: Portable instruments that use a laser or a spark to make the metal emit light can measure carbon in the field, but they need careful surface preparation and calibration.

heading: A grade number is a claim you can check
narration: Often the simplest route is paperwork. In the four-digit grade system widely used in North America, plain carbon steels are numbered beginning with 10, and the last two digits indicate the approximate carbon content in hundredths of a percent.

heading: A grade number is a claim you can check
narration: A grade of 1018 means roughly 0.18 percent carbon, a mild steel.

heading: A grade number is a claim you can check
narration: A grade of 1080 means roughly 0.80 percent carbon, a high-carbon steel.

heading: A grade number is a claim you can check
narration: Steel bought from a mill usually comes with a certificate listing its measured chemistry.

heading: A grade number is a claim you can check
narration: That certificate is a claim, made by someone who ran the analysis, and it can be checked.

heading: A grade number is a claim you can check
narration: Unmarked or reused steel has no such trail, and assumptions about what an old part "must" be made from are guesses until tested.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: As you watch, notice which visuals show a comparison and which show a measurement.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: The spark streams and the skating file are comparisons, judged against known samples.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: The combustion analysis and the spectrometer are measurements, anchored to certified references.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: The magnet appears twice, once as a failed carbon test and once as a working thermometer.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: None of this makes the category sharper than it is. The line at roughly 0.6 percent carbon is a convention, and a steel just either side of it is not meaningfully different in use.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: Workshop tests rank steels; they do not measure them, and alloying elements can mislead both sparks and files.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: Even laboratory numbers describe the sample, not necessarily the whole part. Steel heated in air can lose carbon from its surface, so a spark or a file applied to the skin of a bar may understate what lies beneath.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: Where the sample is taken from matters as much as how it is analysed.

heading: Closing
narration: So the honest answer comes in layers. A magnet tells you almost nothing.

heading: Closing
narration: Sparks and a quench give you a confident ranking. A calibrated chemical analysis gives you the number, and the number is trustworthy because its reference can be traced.
